```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(lme4)
library(apa7)
library(performance)
library(parameters)
apa7_defaults(font_family = "Open Sans", line_spacing = 1.5)
```

```{r}
#| label: setup2
#| eval: false
<<setup>>
```

When observations are nested (trials within participants, students within classrooms) or crossed (participants responding to the same set of items), ordinary regression treats correlated observations as independent and understates uncertainty. Multilevel (mixed-effects) models account for the nesting with random effects. `apa_parameters` accepts models fit with `lme4::lmer`, `lme4::glmer`, `nlme::lme`, and `glmmTMB::glmmTMB` and displays the fixed effects as in an ordinary regression table, followed by the random-effect standard deviations and correlations, each under its own heading.

# Linear Mixed Models

How quickly does performance deteriorate when people do not get enough sleep, and are some people more vulnerable than others? @belenkyPatternsPerformanceDegradation2003 restricted 18 participants to 3 hours of sleep per night and measured their average reaction time on a vigilance task each day. The data are in the `sleepstudy` data set from the lme4 package. Days 0 and 1 were adaptation and training, and Day 2 was the baseline, so we keep Days 2 through 9 and count days of sleep restriction from the baseline.

```{r}
#| label: sleep-data
d_sleep <- sleepstudy |>
  filter(Days >= 2) |>
  mutate(Days = Days - 2) |> 
  rename(Participant = Subject)
```

## How much do participants differ?

A model with only a random intercept for each participant shows how much of the variability in reaction time lies between participants. The intraclass correlation (ICC) is the proportion of the variance that is due to stable differences between participants.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sleep0
#| tbl-cap: "Fit of the Unconditional Model of Reaction Time"
sleep0 <- lmer(Reaction ~ 1 + (1 | Participant), data = d_sleep)
apa_performance(sleep0)
```

About half of the variance in reaction time is between participants, so treating the 144 observations as independent would be a mistake.

Also displayed is the marginal *R*^2^, the proportion of variance explained by fixed effects. Because there are no fixed effects in this model, the *R*^2^~marginal~ is 0. The conditional *R*^2^ is the proportion of variance explained by both fixed and random effects. Because the random effect of participants is the only effect, the *R*^2^~conditional~ is equal to the ICC in this model.

## Random intercepts

The next model adds days of sleep restriction as a fixed effect. Each participant still has their own intercept, but all participants are assumed to slow down at the same rate.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sleep1
#| tbl-cap: "Reaction Time by Days of Sleep Restriction With Random Intercepts"
sleep1 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Participant), 
               data = d_sleep)

apa_parameters(
  sleep1,
  predictor_parameters = c(
    "Parameter", 
    "Coefficient", 
    "SE", "CI", 
    "t", "df_error", "p")
)

```

The table has two parts, each under a heading. The fixed effects are read like ordinary regression coefficients: at baseline, the average reaction time is about 268 ms, and it increases by about 11 ms per day of sleep restriction. Below them, the random effects show the standard deviation (*SD*) of participants' intercepts around the average intercept, and the residual *SD* of observations around each participant's own line.

For linear mixed models, `apa_parameters` tests fixed effects with *t* tests that use Kenward–Roger degrees of freedom, which account for the number of participants as well as the number of observations. Because the intercept and the slope have different degrees of freedom here, they are shown in a *df* column. To use a different method, pass `ci_method` (e.g., `ci_method = "satterthwaite"`, which requires the lmerTest package).

## Random slopes

Do participants differ in how quickly they deteriorate? Adding a random slope for days lets each participant have their own rate of change.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sleep2
#| tbl-cap: "Reaction Time by Days of Sleep Restriction With Random Intercepts and Slopes"
sleep2 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (Days | Participant), 
               data = d_sleep)

apa_parameters(
  sleep2,
  predictor_parameters = c(
    "Parameter", 
    "Coefficient", 
    "SE", "CI", 
    "t", "df_error", "p")
)
```

The average slope is unchanged, but its standard error is larger, because the model now recognizes that participants' slopes vary: the *SD* of the slopes is about 7 ms per day around the average of 11 ms per day. The correlation (*r*) between participants' intercepts and slopes is small. When all fixed effects share the same degrees of freedom, as here, they appear in the *t* column header.

The "Random effects" heading names the statistic of the rows below it (*SD*), and each cluster (here, Participant) has a subheading with its terms indented below it. The correlation names its own statistic (*r*). With several clusters, crossed or nested, each gets its own subheading. With `random_scale = "variance"`, the random effects are variances (*Var*) and covariances (*Cov*) instead:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sleep2-variance
#| tbl-cap: "Random-Slope Model With Random Effects as Variances and Covariances"
apa_parameters(sleep2, random_scale = "variance")
```

The random-effect rows can be omitted with `random = FALSE`, and the "Fixed effects" and "Random effects" headings can be omitted with `effect_headings = FALSE`, in which case each random-effect label names its cluster and statistic (e.g., Participant: *SD* (Days)). Confidence intervals can be added with `"CI"`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sleep2-ci
#| tbl-cap: "Fixed Effects of the Random-Slope Model"
apa_parameters(
  sleep2,
  predictor_parameters = c("Parameter", "Coefficient", "SE", "CI", "t", "df_error", "p"),
  random = FALSE
)
```



## Model fit

For mixed models, `apa_performance` reports the marginal *R*^2^ (the variance explained by the fixed effects), the conditional *R*^2^ (the variance explained by the fixed and random effects together), and the ICC.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sleep2-performance
#| tbl-cap: "Fit of the Random-Slope Model"
apa_performance(sleep2)
```

## Comparing models

A list of mixed models is compared with likelihood ratio tests, and the change in marginal *R*^2^ is shown for each model. When the models differ in their fixed effects, the likelihood ratio test is based on maximum likelihood rather than restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimates, as it should be.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sleep-list
#| apa7-width: landscape
#| tbl-cap: "Three Multilevel Models of Reaction Time"
#| message: false
apa_parameters(list(sleep0, sleep1, sleep2)) |> 
  # as_tibble() |> 
  rename(`Marginal_*R*^2^` = `*R*^2^~marginal~`,
         `Marginal_&Delta;*R*^2^`=`&Delta;*R*^2^~marginal~`,
         `Conditional_*R*^2^` = `*R*^2^~conditional~`,
         `Conditional_&Delta;*R*^2^`=`&Delta;*R*^2^~conditional~`) |> 
  apa_flextable() |> 
  flextable::merge_h_range(i = ~ Model != "", j1 = 1, j2 = 2)
  
```

The random slope does not change the marginal *R*^2^, because the fixed effects are the same in both models, but the likelihood ratio test shows that the slopes vary across participants. 

The comparison can also be displayed on its own with `apa_performance_comparison`, here including the model with no predictors:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sleep-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of Three Multilevel Models of Reaction Time"
#| message: false
apa_performance_comparison(list(sleep0, sleep1, sleep2)) |>
  apa_flextable()
```

## Correlated residuals with nlme

lme4 assumes that, after the random effects are taken into account, a participant's residuals are independent. In daily measurements, though, a participant who is unusually slow on one day is often unusually slow the next day too. The nlme package can model such residual correlation. Here the random-slope model is refit with `nlme::lme` and a first-order autoregressive (AR(1)) correlation among each participant's residuals:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sleep-lme
#| tbl-cap: "Random-Slope Model With First-Order Autoregressive Residuals"
sleep_lme <- nlme::lme(
  Reaction ~ Days,
  random = ~ Days | Participant,
  correlation = nlme::corAR1(),
  data = d_sleep
)
tbl_sleep_lme <- apa_parameters(sleep_lme)
tbl_sleep_lme
```

The fixed effects are tested with *t* tests whose degrees of freedom are computed by nlme from the grouping levels at which each effect varies, rather than with Kenward–Roger degrees of freedom. The parameters of the residual structure are shown below the residual *SD*: residuals on adjacent days correlate about .45. The table note names the structure:

```{r}
#| label: sleep-lme-note
apa_note(tbl_sleep_lme)
```

Because the AR(1) structure and the random slopes both describe how a participant's reaction times hang together over days, they compete with each other: with correlated residuals, the intercept *SD* is smaller and the correlation between intercepts and slopes is nearly 1, a sign that these data cannot fully separate the two. A likelihood ratio test compares the model with and without correlated residuals:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sleep-lme-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of Models With Independent and Autoregressive Residuals"
#| message: false
sleep_lme0 <- nlme::lme(
  Reaction ~ Days,
  random = ~ Days | Participant,
  data = d_sleep
)
apa_performance_comparison(
  list(`Independent residuals` = sleep_lme0, `AR(1) residuals` = sleep_lme)
)
```

Variance functions (the `weights` argument, e.g., `nlme::varIdent(form = ~ 1 | Group)` for a separate residual *SD* in each group) are displayed the same way, with a row for each parameter and a sentence in the note.

# Generalized Linear Mixed Models

`glmer` models are displayed like `glm` models, with exponentiated coefficients (e.g., odds ratios) and *z* tests for the fixed effects.

The `VerbAgg` data set from the lme4 package contains 316 people's responses to 24 items describing verbally aggressive reactions to frustrating situations. Each item describes a behavior (cursing, scolding, or shouting) in a situation in which someone else is to blame or in which the respondent is to blame, and asks whether the respondent would *want* to react that way or would actually *do* so. Do people with higher trait anger endorse more verbally aggressive reactions, and are people less willing to say that they would act aggressively than that they would want to?

Because every person responds to every item, people and items are crossed random effects.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-verbagg
#| tbl-cap: "Logistic Mixed Model of Endorsing Verbally Aggressive Reactions"
d_va <- VerbAgg |>
  mutate(
    Response = r2 == "Y",
    Gender = factor(Gender, labels = c("Female", "Male")),
    Behavior = btype,
    Mode = mode,
    Situation = situ,
    Person = id,
    Item = item
  )

glmer_va <- glmer(
  Response ~ Anger + Gender + Behavior + Mode + Situation +
    (1 | Person) + (1 | Item),
  data = d_va,
  family = binomial,
  control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)
apa_parameters(glmer_va)
```

Each point of trait anger multiplies the odds of endorsing an item by about 1.06. Scolding and shouting are endorsed less often than cursing, reactions are endorsed less often when the respondent is to blame than when someone else is, and people are less likely to say they would *do* something than that they would *want* to. The random-effect *SD*s are on the log-odds scale and show that people differ much more than items do, after the item characteristics are taken into account.

# Count Outcomes with glmmTMB

Counts often vary more than a Poisson model allows (overdispersion) or have more zeros than it predicts. The [glmmTMB](https://glmmtmb.github.io/glmmTMB/) package fits mixed models for such data, including negative binomial models and models with a separate zero-inflation part. `apa_parameters` displays them like `glmer` models.

In this made-up daily-diary study, 120 adults who drink heavily recorded the number of alcoholic drinks they had each day for 2 weeks. Half of them had been assigned to a brief intervention and half to a control condition. Do people in the intervention drink less, and do they drink more on weekends?

```{r}
#| label: drinks-data
set.seed(12)
n_people <- 120
people <- tibble(
  Person = factor(1:n_people),
  Condition = factor(rep(c("Control", "Intervention"), each = n_people / 2)),
  person_effect = rnorm(n_people, mean = 0, sd = .6)
)

d_drinks <- tidyr::expand_grid(people, `Diary Day` = 1:14) |>
  mutate(
    Day = factor(`Diary Day` %% 7 %in% c(6, 0), labels = c("Weekday", "Weekend")),
    intervention = Condition == "Intervention",
    # Expected drinks on a drinking day
    mu = exp(log(2.5) - .5 * intervention + .6 * (Day == "Weekend") + person_effect),
    # Some days are abstinent days, more often in the intervention
    abstinent = rbinom(n(), 1, plogis(-1.2 + intervention)),
    Drinks = ifelse(
      abstinent == 1,
      0,
      rnbinom(n(), size = ifelse(intervention, 1, 3), mu = mu)
    )
  ) |>
  select(Person, Condition, `Diary Day`, Day, Drinks)
```

The counts have a mean of `r round(mean(d_drinks$Drinks), 2)` but a variance of `r round(var(d_drinks$Drinks), 2)`, and `r round(100 * mean(d_drinks$Drinks == 0))`% of them are zeros, far more variability than a Poisson model allows.

## Negative binomial models

A negative binomial model adds a dispersion parameter that lets the variance grow faster than the mean. People are a random effect, because each person reported on many days.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-drinks-nb
#| tbl-cap: "Negative Binomial Mixed Model of Daily Drinks"
tmb_nb <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(
  Drinks ~ Condition + Day + (1 | Person),
  family = glmmTMB::nbinom2,
  data = d_drinks
)
apa_parameters(tmb_nb)
```

As with `glmer`, coefficients are tested with *z* tests, and coefficients of models with a log link are exponentiated. For count models, the exponentiated coefficients are incidence rate ratios (*IRR*): people in the intervention had about half as many drinks as people in the control condition, and people had almost twice as many drinks on weekends as on weekdays. The person *SD* is on the log scale. The dispersion parameter itself is not displayed, because it is not tested.

## Zero-inflated models

Another account of the many zeros is that some days are abstinent days, on which a person would not drink at all, while on the other days the number of drinks varies as usual. A zero-inflated model has two parts: a conditional model of the counts, and a logistic model of whether a zero is one of these excess zeros. Here a zero-inflated Poisson model lets the probability of an excess zero differ between the conditions:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-drinks-zip
#| tbl-cap: "Zero-Inflated Poisson Mixed Model of Daily Drinks"
tmb_zip <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(
  Drinks ~ Condition + Day + (1 | Person),
  ziformula = ~ Condition,
  family = poisson,
  data = d_drinks
)
tbl_zip <- apa_parameters(tmb_zip)
tbl_zip
```

Each part of the model has its own heading, with its fixed and random effects under subheadings. Only the conditional model's coefficients are exponentiated, because the zero-inflation coefficients are log odds: the probability of an excess zero is about `r zi <- glmmTMB::fixef(tmb_zip)$zi; sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.2f", plogis(zi[1])))` in the control condition (the inverse logit of `r sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", zi[1]))`) and `r sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.2f", plogis(sum(zi))))` in the intervention (the inverse logit of `r sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", zi[1]))` + `r sprintf("%.2f", zi[2])`). People in the intervention had more abstinent days and somewhat fewer drinks on the other days. The table note says what the zero-inflation coefficients are:

```{r}
#| label: drinks-zip-note
apa_note(tbl_zip)
```

The two models explain the zeros differently, and their *AIC*s can be compared with `apa_performance`. Here the negative binomial model fits better:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-drinks-aic
#| tbl-cap: "Information Criteria of the Negative Binomial and Zero-Inflated Poisson Models"
apa_performance(
  list(`Negative binomial` = tmb_nb, `Zero-inflated Poisson` = tmb_zip),
  metrics = c("AIC", "BIC")
)
```

## Dispersion models

With `dispformula`, the dispersion parameter itself is modeled, and the table has a "Dispersion model" part. For negative binomial models, a larger dispersion parameter means less overdispersion, so the negative coefficient here means that the counts of people in the intervention are more overdispersed: many of their days have no drinks, but some have many. As the note says, dispersion coefficients are on the log scale.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-drinks-disp
#| tbl-cap: "Negative Binomial Mixed Model With Dispersion Depending on Condition"
glmmTMB::glmmTMB(
  Drinks ~ Condition + Day + (1 | Person),
  dispformula = ~ Condition,
  family = glmmTMB::nbinom2,
  data = d_drinks
) |>
  apa_parameters()
```

## Fit and comparisons

`apa_performance` reports the marginal and conditional *R*^2^ and the ICC of glmmTMB models, and nested models are compared with likelihood ratio tests, as for lme4 models:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-drinks-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of Models of Daily Drinks With and Without Day of the Week"
tmb_nb0 <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(
  Drinks ~ Condition + (1 | Person),
  family = glmmTMB::nbinom2,
  data = d_drinks
)
apa_performance_comparison(
  list(`Condition` = tmb_nb0, `Condition and day` = tmb_nb)
)
```
